Subject: GPU runway and scaleback choreography — ZenBridge dedicated sizing

Kyle —

Great talking yesterday. Per our conversation, I wanted to put a short note capturing the proposal for Dedicated capacity behavior tied to ZenBridge's expected traffic patterns. High level: we recommend a "runway + scaleback" choreography rather than fixed aggressive overprovisioning — that is, a small committed baseline sized for 95th percentile steady-state with a short runway window that allows rapid scale-up for short-lived spikes, plus a controlled scaleback policy to avoid noisy neighbor effects.

Key asks from your side for the sizing exercise:
- hourly and 5-min request QPS distribution for the last 90 days (if available)
- percent of requests that are low-latency (<200ms target) vs batch
- preferred times for scheduled high-throughput jobs (nightly / weekly)

Proposed attachments I will share once we align: a one-page runbook for ops (scale triggers, cooldowns, preemption tolerance) and a spreadsheet with runway math.

Can you send over the usage histogram and confirm procurement can accept a short uplift window for ephemeral capacity charges? I’ll loop in Karthik and Kim with the operational thresholds.

Thanks,
Jordan
Account Exec, Redwood Inference

Jordan —

Thanks for the summary. Attached is a high-level extract of our request patterns (we've redacted some user ids). Short version:
- 70% of traffic is steady interactive inference (mostly <250ms target)
- 20% is bursty evaluation traffic (spikes that last 10–30 minutes)
- 10% are scheduled large-batch jobs (mostly between 02:00–04:00 local)

Procurement: we need clear caps on overage exposure — they don't want unlimited uplift charges. If you can propose a capped runway pricing band (e.g., runway allowances per month, with soft and hard caps), that would help.

I'll leave the technical thresholds to your ops folks, but priority is preserving interactive latency during spikes.

—Kyle

Subject: Re: GPU runway and scaleback choreography — ZenBridge dedicated sizing

Kyle — Jordan looped me in for the SLA/pricing side. Based on the pattern you shared, here is a pragmatic construct we can put in the SOW appendix:

1) Baseline committed capacity sized to 95th percentile steady QPS. This is billed as the Dedicated monthly commitment.
2) Runway allowance: we provide a monthly pool of "runway minutes" (e.g., 24,000 GPU-minutes) which can be used for rapid uplift. Runway consumption is metered and priced at an uplift rate significantly below on-demand to discourage waste, capped at a defined monthly maximum.
3) Hard cap and soft cap: Soft cap triggers Tier 1 alerts and auto-scale continues. If runway consumption reaches the hard cap, Redwood will notify and throttle new uplift requests; interactive traffic will be shifted to a pre-agreed compatible model variant with slightly higher latency to preserve availability.
4) Scaleback choreography: quick scale-up (30–90s median for warm pools), followed by staged scale-down with a cooldown window (default 15 minutes) plus an option to increase cooldown for specific scheduled batch windows.

We can include an overage protection clause: if procurement requests a firm dollars cap, Redwood can offer an escrow-credited buffer (one-time funded buffer that behaves like pre-purchased runway minutes) in exchange for a modest contract uplift.

I'll attach a draft terms sheet for you to review. If procurement prefers a percent-based cap instead of minutes, we can convert minutes into a nominal dollar cap.

Karthik
Director, Strategic Accounts — Redwood Inference

Kyle — quick ops note on the "runway" mechanics and how we keep your interactive latency intact during short spikes:

- Warm pool vs cold add: we keep a small pool of warm KV-cache-bearing instances per model to hit <250ms on first token for interactive requests. For true scale-ups, we use pre-initialized nodes with checkpoints to reduce warm time to ~30–60s for standard models.
- Traffic shaping: requests are staged into priority queues — interactive requests get preemption protection; evaluation and batch jobs are bumped to best-effort queues during spikes. This keeps tail latency predictable.
- Cooldown and grace windows: default cooldown 15m, but for nightly batch windows we can set a longer cooldown to avoid churn.
- Telemetry + Handoff: We'll provide a runbook with run-rate thresholds (QPS per model), a dashboard playbook (token-level cost), and a webhook for immediate alerting to your on-call.

Attachment: ops_runbook_excerpt.txt (txt stub)

If you can share the per-model QPS (sample) we’ll mark which models require warm pools vs best-effort.

Kim
Sr. Ops Product Manager, Redwood Inference

Team —

This looks good and aligned to what our infra team needs. Procurement reviewed Karthik's options; they prefer the runway-minutes model with a monthly hard cap (dollars converted from minutes). They asked for two items before legal signs off:
1) a one-page schedule showing how runway minutes convert to dollar spend under normal vs uplift rates, and
2) confirmation that interactive traffic will not be throttled below our SLA except in the event of a hard cap breach, and that Redwood will send a 6-hour advance notice before throttling.

Next steps: Jordan — can you 1) send the spreadsheet populated with our histogram + runway math, 2) share the one-page schedule tying minutes -> dollars, and 3) set up a 45-minute technical handoff with your ops team (Kim) and our infra engineers for next Tue? Procurement wants DocuSign links after those items are in.

Appreciate the quick turnaround — happy to move to an LOI if the numbers grid.

—Kyle
VP of Infrastructure, ZenBridge
